parts.title: Muscle Loss
parts.article:
Muscle Loss
 
A For people confined to bed for long periods of time, or for astronauts in microgravity, muscle wasting is a serious problem. Wasting, or atrophy, is a symptom not only of disuse and injury, but of many diseases, including kidney failure, cancer and AIDS. Once enough muscle has been lost, a vicious cycle sets in as exercise becomes increasingly difficult, which in turn leads to disuse and further atrophy.
 
B Despite more than three decades of research into alternatives, the only way to stop such patients losing muscle is a long course of physiotherapy involving weight-bearing exercise, but this is of little use to the weakest and sickest—and in most cases, starts only after wasting has already set in. The use of anabolic steroids is being explored for some conditions. But these compounds have a huge range of effects on the body besides promoting muscle growth, some of them undesirable, and only appear to work well in conjunction with exercise.
 
C Alfred Goldberg, a cell biologist at Harvard University, began studying muscle atrophy in the late 1960s. What he and others discovered was that, rather than being a passive side effect of disuse or disease, muscle wasting is an active process controlled by a complex genetic pathway. So, if someone found out how it was turned on, it ought to be possible to turn it off. “Back then we didn't know the pathway for muscle breakdown,” says Goldberg, “but about five years ago our work showed that no matter what the trigger—disuse, metabolic disease or fasting—the same biochemical programme is responsible.”
 
D The process involves the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (UPP), the disposal machinery used to break down unwanted proteins in the cell (New Scientist, 17 December 2005, p. 36). Once the system has been activated, ubiquitin “destroy me” labels are added to muscle proteins. This breaks down the muscle filaments within cells, but does not change the number of muscle cells. Instead, they become thinner and weaker.
Further studies showed that at least 90 genes are involved in atrophy; Goldberg calls them “atrogenes.” Although it is still unknown which of these genes triggers atrophy, it soon became clear that two of them are essential to the process. Atrogin1 and muRF1 were first described in 2001 and are the only two atrogenes active only during muscle atrophy. They code for ubiquitin ligases, the enzymes that attach the “destroy me” labels to proteins. The genes are barely active in normal muscle, but expression levels shoot up in sick animals. Knock out either, and muscle wasting all but stops.
 
E An experiment was conducted on a “superboy” who was normal at birth, lacking fat; by the age of five, he was excellent at weightlifting, lifting as much as three kilograms. The scientists found that this is closely related to his mother, who is a professional runner, and that his extended family has unusually strong abilities. The boy's condition is caused by a lack of myostatin, a protein that normally limits muscle growth. Without it, muscles grow far larger and stronger than usual. But the drug can have a temporary effect.
 
F There are still many gaps to be filled in, but those in the field agree that the question is no longer if we can develop anti-wasting treatments, but when. As researchers close in on this target, excitement is mounting about exactly what such treatments could achieve. Patients due to be confined to bed for more than a few days could be given the drug as soon as they begin bed rest to prevent muscle loss that would otherwise slow their recovery. Weaning patients off respirators would become easier as doctors could prevent wasting of the diaphragm. Disease need no longer lead to weakness, and broken bones would not mean long and painful physiotherapy sessions to rebuild muscle strength. And since loss of muscle mass is a major reason why we grow frail with age, an anti-wasting drug could keep older people on their feet and living independently for longer.
 
G The prospect of preventing atrophy is also of great interest to NASA, particularly in view of its much talked-about mission to Mars. By the time astronauts reach the Red Planet, they can expect to lose up to 25 per cent of their muscle mass and be too weak to walk, let alone put on a space suit and carry out repairs. That is why Goldberg's work is funded by the National Space Biomedical Research Institute in Houston, Texas, set up by NASA.
 
H While there are valid medical and space applications for anti-wasting drugs, as a safer alternative to steroids they will inevitably be hugely tempting for athletes too, not to mention the lazy as well. Although Goldberg is keen to point out that helping cheats and couch potatoes is not the focus of his work, he admits that it will undoubtedly happen sooner or later.

questions.question: A description of a boy with unusual muscle strength

analyses.content: 题目要求找到对一个肌肉力量异常的男孩的描述。原文 E 段 开头明确提到对一个“superboy（超级男孩）”进行了实验，他五岁时就擅长“weightlifting（举重）”。
看到 “superboy” 和 “weightlifting” 即可锁定该段落。
(Paragraph E) “An experiment was conducted on a 'superboy'... by the age of five, he was excellent at weightlifting...”

questions.question: A reference to the limitations of current treatments for muscle loss

analyses.content: 题目要求找到提及目前肌肉流失治疗方法的局限性。原文 B 段 提到物理治疗（physiotherapy）对最虚弱的人没用（little use），以及类固醇（anabolic steroids）有副作用（undesirable effects）且仅在配合运动时有效。
“Limitations” 对应原文的 “little use” 和 “undesirable... only appear to work well in conjunction with exercise”。
(Paragraph B) “...but this is of little use to the weakest... some of them undesirable...”

questions.question: A mention of a space agency's interest in anti-wasting research

analyses.content: (Paragraph G) “The prospect of preventing atrophy is also of great interest to NASA...”
题目要求找到提及航天局对抗萎缩研究的兴趣。原文 G 段 第一句就提到预防萎缩的前景对 NASA（美国国家航空航天局）非常感兴趣。
NASA 即题目中的 “space agency”。

questions.question: A reason why space travel could lead to severe muscle loss

analyses.content: A段第一句话明确给出了太空旅行导致肌肉萎缩的根本原因：宇航员处于“微重力（microgravity）”环境之中。
注意！你可能会因为看到G段提到了去火星会失去25%的肌肉而错选G，但G段描述的是流失的“严重程度”和背景，真正点出“原因（reason）”的是A段中的科学名词“microgravity（微重力）”。
For people confined to bed for long periods of time, or for astronauts in microgravity, muscle wasting is a serious problem.

questions.question: An explanation of the biological process that causes muscle breakdown

analyses.content: 题目要求找到解释导致肌肉分解的生物过程。原文 D 段 详细描述了 UPP（泛素-蛋白酶体途径）如何给蛋白质贴上 “destroy me”（毁灭我）的标签并进行分解。
“Biological process” 对应原文的 “biochemical programme” 和 “pathway”。
(Paragraph D) “The process involves the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (UPP)... ubiquitin 'destroy me' labels are added...”

questions.question: A prediction of the wide-ranging benefits of anti-wasting drugs

analyses.content: 题目要求找到预测抗萎缩药物的广泛益处。原文 F 段 列举了药物若研发成功后的多种用途：帮助卧床病人康复、帮助病人脱离呼吸机、帮助老年人独立生活等。
H 段预测的是抗萎缩药物可能被运动员和懒人滥用的负面影响，而 19 题要求选出段落包含 “wide-ranging benefits of anti-wasting drugs” （药物的益处），因此不能选 H 段。
(Paragraph F) “...prevent muscle loss that would otherwise slow their recovery. Weaning patients off respirators would become easier...”

analyses.content: 题目说研究显示超级男孩出生时几乎没有____。原文 E 段 提到：“superboy who was normal at birth, lacking fat（出生时正常，缺乏脂肪）”。
“Very little” 对应原文的 “lacking”。
(Paragraph E) “...superboy who was normal at birth, lacking fat...”
题目说五岁时，他能举起多达____。原文 E 段 提到：“lifting as much as three kilograms（举起多达三公斤）”。
题目要求填一个词（ONE WORD ONLY）。虽然口语中 “lift up to three” 听起来缺单位，但在雅思填空规则下，提取核心数字词 three 是正确做法。
(Paragraph E) “...lifting as much as three kilograms.”
题目说他的母亲是一名____。原文 E 段 提到：“his mother, who is a professional runner（他的母亲，一位职业赛跑选手）”。
“Works as a” 对应原文 “is a professional”。
(Paragraph E) “...his mother, who is a professional runner...”
题目说他家庭的其他成员拥有____强大的力量。原文 E 段 提到：“extended family has unusually strong abilities（大家庭有异常强的能力）”。
题目结构是 “have ______ great strength”（副词+形容词）。原文是 “unusually strong”（副词+形容词）。
(Paragraph E) “...extended family has unusually strong abilities.”
题目说这种情况与缺乏____有关。原文 E 段 倒数第二句提到：“The boy's condition is caused by a lack of myostatin（这个男孩的情况是由缺乏肌肉生长抑制素引起的）”。
题目 “linked to a lack of” 直接对应原文 “caused by a lack of”。
(Paragraph E) “The boy's condition is caused by a lack of myostatin...”
